Thai massaman beef curry
42 ratings

    Prep
    10m
    Cook
    1h 40m
    Serves
    4

Thai massaman beef curry
Image by (N/A)
Jump to
Recipe
Reviews
Coles Magazine
Coles Magazine Updated on: 01/06/26
This recipe was originally published in the Coles Magazine and republished here with permission

Of all the curries that Thailand has to offer, massaman is the most intriguing. Also spelt mussaman, this curry has a mysterious complex flavour due to the addition of woody spices to the usual fresh ingredients of lemongrass, galangal, chilli and garlic that form the base of a Thai curry. This recipe ticks all the boxes for a great massaman curry; the onion is cut into thick wedges, acting as a vegetable, along with the potato, as well as an aromatic, and the beef is slowly cooked until meltingly tender in both coconut milk and beef stock providing enough soupy broth to soak up the rice. The classic Thai flavours of sweet, sour, spicy and salty are represented by palm sugar, lime, chilli and fish sauce. Use this as a base and start playing around with your proteins, like lamb shanks, chicken or even duck or goat!
Read more
Cook Mode
Prevent your screen from going dark
Ingredients (19)

    1 tbsp vegetable oil
    1 brown onion, cut into large wedges
    1/3 cup (100g) massaman curry paste
    1kg Coles Australian Beef Chuck Casserole Steak, cut into 5cm pieces
    1 garlic clove, crushed
    1 tbsp finely grated ginger
    400ml can coconut milk
    1/2 cup (125ml) beef stock
    1 cinnamon stick or quill
    1 long red chilli, thinly sliced
    2 bay leaves
    2 tbsp palm sugar
    2 tbsp lime juice
    1 tbsp fish sauce
    1/3 cup (45g) roasted unsalted peanuts
    400g potatoes, peeled, quartered
    Steamed jasmine rice, to serve
    Coriander sprigs, to serve
    Lime wedges, to serve

$19 per serve
i
Estimate based on regular price of ingredients at Coles Burwood East, VIC
Fulfilled by coles-logo
Allergens

Recipe may contain: peanuts, tree nuts, milk, fish and shellfish.

Disclaimer: Always read product labels to ensure the products in the recipe suit your needs if you have allergies or intolerances.
Method
Show ingredient quantity

    Step 1
    Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pan over medium-low heat. Add the onion and cook for 5 mins. Add massaman paste and cook for 1 min or until fragrant. Add the beef and cook, stirring, for 3 mins or until browned. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 1 min.
    Step 2
    Add coconut milk, stock, cinnamon, chilli, bay leaves, palm sugar, lime juice, fish sauce, peanuts and potato to the pan and bring to the boil. Reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer for 1 1/2 hours or until the beef is very tender.
    Step 3
    Divide the steamed jasmine rice among serving bowls. Top with the curry and serve with coriander and lime wedges.

Recipe notes
What is palm sugar?

Palm sugar is the concentrated sap of sugar palm trees. Not unlike maple syrup, cuts are made in the trunks of the trees and pipes are inserted. The sap then slowly flows out from the tree. This sap is then boiled and reduced to a thick syrup which is then dried out in the sun. Palm sugar varies in colour due to weather conditions and how long the palm syrup is simmered. The darker the colour the deeper the caramel flavour will be. Although it can sometimes be bought in a granulated form, palm sugar is more commonly sold in a block and can be shaved or grated before adding to your dish. If unavailable, brown sugar is a good substitute although not as deep and molasses-ey.
What is the difference between massaman and panang curries?

At face value, both these curries are pretty much the same, containing red curry paste, coconut milk and peanuts. There are, however, a few differences. Massaman is heavier on spices, with penang only having a pinch or so of cumin, coriander or nutmeg. A major distinction is that panang isn’t a Muslim dish, so you can have it with thinly sliced pork added at the end.
What are the origins of Massaman curry?

One of the reasons massaman curry tastes so exotic, is because it is! While there are differing stories of how it developed, we do know that it is the result of influences from different parts of the world. Part Persian, with perhaps a touch of India plus influences for the southern Thai Muslim population and then what the northern Thais added to it. Massaman comes from the Persian word for Muslim, moselman. The spices added may include cardamom, cumin, cinnamon, coriander, nutmeg, cloves and star anise.
What do you serve with Massaman curry?

Indian curries are served with little sides like raita, mango chutney and kachumber. With Thai curries, the extra flavourings are served on top, like fresh coriander or basil and lime wedges. Serve you massaman curry with steamed rice (make sure it's jasmine rice) or maybe pay homage to its Persian and Indian origins by serving it with flatbread.
What is the difference between coconut milk and coconut cream?

Just as dairy has both milk and cream, so does coconut. Coconut milk and cream is the pulverised flesh from coconuts, mixed with water and then pureed. Coconut cream has a higher fat content than coconut milk, containing less water making it thicker. Coconut milk has a higher water content. It’s up to you which one you use, knowing the coconut cream will make your massaman thicker and richer.
